source.title: FlipAttack: Jailbreak LLMs via Flipping
source.authors: Yue Liu; Xiao-Xin He; Miao Xiong; Jin-Lan Fu; Shu-Min Deng; Ying-Wei Ma; Jia-Heng Zhang; Bryan Hooi

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendix are present. Some text has extraction/OCR artifacts, but the relevant tables are legible.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports jailbreak and prompt-understanding experiments, but does not test the listed fine-tuning, first-token KL, compliant-prefill/suffix/decoding, localization, shallowness-cause, or deepening claims. Its flipping attack is a different prompt-transformation method.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports harmful-completion attack success rates for FlipAttack on eight models; these are relevant to the broader subject of safety behavior but do not test any listed claim version's intervention or mechanism. Table 21 reports aggregate attack success rates with system-prompt and perplexity-filter defenses. Perplexity, tokenization, guard-model bypass, and benign prompt-reconstruction results do not measure the claim versions' specified safety behavior. Baseline attack comparisons are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: FlipAttack is a black-box prompt-transformation jailbreak on deployed chat models. It runs no fine-tuning, first-token KL, prefill/suffix/decoding test, localization, or deepening experiment, so it bears on none of V1-V7. Its one-query attack success rates (Table 1, Table 21) are a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors conclude FlipAttack jailbreaks LLMs in one query (78.97% average ASR-GPT over 8 models, about 98% bypass of 5 guard models). They attribute this to left-to-right understanding and the stealth of flipped text. They say the simple defenses are ineffective or only partly effective.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses prompt transformation and flipping guidance for a black-box jailbreak attack, rather than fine-tuning, token-position KL measurement, or safety-depth training.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by model and by flipping mode and guidance variant; the paper also reports changes under system-prompt and perplexity-filter defenses.

fits_no_version.finding: FlipAttack gets ASR-GPT of 27.50% to 94.04% on 8 chat models in Table 1, averaging 78.97%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A prompt-transformation attack that disguises harmful requests and guides the model to recover them can elicit harmful completions from tested chat models, with success varying widely across models.

fits_no_version.finding: In Table 21 the average ASR-GPT is 81.76% for FlipAttack alone, 82.33% with SPD and 74.40% with PGF.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A safety system prompt does not reduce FlipAttack success, and a perplexity filter reduces it only modestly at a 4% benign rejection rate.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267 (2025)
record.problems: The main attack results use GPT-4-based evaluation; the paper reports that evaluation methods differ in agreement with human labels. No uncertainty estimates are given for the main ASRs. The authors note reduced effectiveness on some models and harmful-behavior categories, and that few-shot examples can expose harmful content.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted due to the row cap. Not extracted as rows: ASRs for other attack methods in Tables 1, 6–8; guard-model bypass counts/rates; perplexity and tokenization measurements; benign flipping match rates; and per-model defense results in Table 21, because they are comparisons or measures outside the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No compliant prefill, adversarial suffix or decoding change. The paper cites GCG as a white-box baseline, but its transferred suffix results are baseline comparisons, not tests of V4.
No test of data or objective as the cause of shallowness. The paper's speculation about few flipped instructions in training data concerns understanding, not safety depth.

record.verdict_notes: Row r10 and r11 baselines (81.76%) come from Table 21, a different configuration from Table 1 (78.97%). Rows r1-r11 should stay linked to none. The state cannot_determine is acceptable because no version is tested. Main ASRs come from GPT-4 judging with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning or change in refusal after fine-tuning.
No benign-data fine-tuning or change in harmful compliance after training.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement on harmful prompts.
No compliant response prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test, and no test of whether bypassing initial response tokens explains safety failures.
No weight or rank localization/editing test of safety behavior.
No test of how safety-training data or objectives cause shallow safety behavior.
No training to deepen safety across response tokens or test of whether such training holds up.
